name: Old Mon
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress; 1 further work by the same author (or citing it for stress) agrees.
catalog_citation: Blagden, C. O. 1920. Môn Inscriptions: General Introduction. In Chas. Duroiselle (ed.), Epigraphia Birmanica, Vol. I, Part II, pp. 69-84. Rangoon: Superintendent, Government Printing. Supplemented by Blagden, C. O. 1914. Talaing, Mon and Ramannadesa (Etymological Notes). Journal of the Burma Research Society 4: 57-60.
catalog_locator: Epigraphia Birmanica I.II p. 71 fn. 1 (scan p. 80), p. 80 §16 (scan p. 89) and p. 81 §17 (scan p. 90); JBRS 4 (1914) p. 59 (scan p. 82)
catalog_quote: [EB I.II p. 71 fn. 1] Probably pronounced Rĕmán, i.e. with a short neutral vowel in the first syllable and the accent on the final syllable (as usual in Môn words). See J. Burma Research S., 1914, pp. 59, 60; 1915, p. 27. [p. 80 §16] Theoretically, the vowel a is, as in other Indian alphabets, inherent in the consonants in general, unless negatived expressly ... As a matter of fact the actual sound is not always a, and even in the early period it is probable that in syllables preceding the final one the inherent sound was really a short neutral vowel (something like the a in abide). [Blagden 1914, JBRS 4: 59] The form Rman, which occurs repeatedly in the Kalyani inscription of Pegu (late 15th century A. D.), must have been pronounced with some short indeterminate vowel between the R and the m. It is quite usual in the early Mon inscriptions to find two or even three consonants piled up together at the beginning of a word in such a way that they could not possibly have been pronounced as they stand. One must supply a short vowel, for which the Mon alphabet neither found a symbol in its Indian prototype nor troubled to invent one. Therefore we may take it that Rman was pronounced something like Rĕmán with the vowel of the first syllable pretty much like the final a in the English word "Africa" and with the stress on the last syllable.
world_status: statement found in an open source

T…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Old Mon words are monosyllables or a main syllable preceded by one (rarely two) presyllables; the accent falls on the final (main) syllable, and the vowel of any preceding syllable was a short neutral (schwa-like) vowel already in the early (Old Mon) inscriptions, its spelling (a ~ i ~ u) being non-distinctive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing in Blagden. (Shorto 1971: 184f., as quoted by Jenny 2005: 137, speaks of '(secondary) stress in final position' for the clause-final particle da < das, i.e. phrase-level prominence, not word-internal secondary stress.)
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Indic (Sanskrit/Pali) loans keep polysyllabic learned shapes in spelling; Blagden notes only that the inherent vowel is 'not always a'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, inferred from orthography of a dead epigraphic language (Pagan-period 'early Môn', 11th-12th c.) plus the author's knowledge of medieval and modern Mon ('as usual in Môn words'); the footnote's example Rmañ is a medieval-Mon form. Modern descriptions of spoken Mon (Jenny 2019: 282; Huffman 1990: 39) and Shorto's OM analysis relayed by Bauer 1990: 159, 164 agree: unstressed presyllable + stressed main syllable, phrase-final prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Blagden's 'early Môn' is the Old Mon of the 11th-12th c. Pagan/Prome inscriptions in Burma (Shwezigon, Myazedi etc.), i.e. classical Old Mon, not specifically the 6th-10th c. Dvaravati Old Mon of Thailand that Glottolog's oldm1242 coordinates point to; ISO omx / oldm1242 covers both stages. His footnote remark 'as usual in Môn words' generalises over Mon of all periods (he also knew modern Mon, monn1252). Any stress statement for Old Mon is necessarily inferential (dead epigraphic language): it rests on orthographic vowel neutralisation in presyllables plus the iambic pattern of modern Mon and Nyah Kur.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: also confirmed is held by the project (294 pp., image-only, no text on p. 82). The passage sits on printed p. 59, section 'II. Mon and Ramaññadesa', the scanned text. The page scan reads exactly: 'The form Rman, which occurs repeatedly in the Kalyani inscription of Pegu (late 15th century A. D.), must have been pronounced with some short indeterminate vowel between the R and the m. It is quite usual in the early Mon inscriptions to find two or even three consonants piled up together at the beginning of a word in such a way that they could not possibly have been pronounced as they stand. One must supply a short vowel, for which the Mon alphabet neither found a symbol in its Indian prototype…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (final stress, final) and the existing Blagden 1920 statement (fixed: final syllable); this is the earlier, single-word form of the same claim by the same author, with the same 'Africa'-final-a description of the unstressed presyllable vowel. Adds nothing on secondary stress, weight or exceptions. The word cited (Rman) is from the Kalyani inscription (late 15th c., strictly Middle Mon), though Blagden ties it to the 11th-c. form Rmeñ and to 'the early Mon inscriptions' generally.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-initial consonant piles in the early Mon inscriptions were pronounced with an inserted short neutral vowel (schwa-like, as the final a of English 'Africa'), and the stress fell on the last syllable: Rman = Rĕmán. The statement is made for one word (the ethnonym) and generalised only for the presyllable vowel, not explicitly for stress; the explicit generalisation 'accent on the final syllable (as usual in Mon words)' comes in Blagden 1920 (Epigraphia Birmanica I.2, p. 71 fn. 1), which cites this 1914 note.
new_statements.identity_note: The one work is an etymological note, not a grammar; its stress remark concerns the ethnonym Rman as written in the Kalyani inscription of Pegu (late 15th century, i.e. Middle Mon in Shorto's periodisation) and in earlier records (11th-c. Rmeñ). Blagden's remark about consonant piles needing a supplied short vowel is stated for 'the early Mon inscriptions' generally. Another Blagden note in the same volume (p. 138, on Duroiselle's transliteration of the 1100 A.D. Mon inscriptions) speaks of 'the main stress' being on the first part of the diphthongs aw/ay, which is about diphthong structure, not word stress, and is not a listed work.
